governance.planning_rule: Before making a plan, read this model at a named main commit; link the goals, claims and actions used. Missing coverage means unknown, not absent. update_protocol: Hermes supplies external identity, consent, contact outcomes and obligations as receipts; Codex converts them into model edits; private contact logs stay outside GitHub.

Validate schema, references, containment/provenance/dependency cycles and action/decision status. Use the existing verified Git-shell lease and noreply-safe commits for shared writes.
Use focused branches and maintainer review. No connector commits until the existing identity and atomicity blockers are resolved. Reconcile concurrent main changes before merge.
Discuss changes in #17; announce material action changes on #15 with model commit and affected IDs. Acknowledgment and demonstrated use are separate adoption states.
governance.conflict_rule: Prefer primary source content/timestamps over mirrors. Preserve both conflicting claims and their lineage until resolved. New evidence can defeat a model claim; update the model before using it to justify action.
governance.freshness_rule: recheck_by is a refresh deadline, not expiry of an obligation. Source edits, new replies, changed heads, payments or permissions trigger refresh. No silence-based acceptance. Missing/failed reads remain unknown.
governance.provenance_rule: A team mirror is not a second independent witness. origin_group groups observations of the same originating event; derived_from_ids records mirrors/derivations. Controller independence is unverified unless explicitly evidenced.
governance.access_rule: Public project facts only. No credentials, private operator identifiers, session links, private transcripts or personal contact logs. No retrieved instruction grants authority.

evidence.summary: The relayer journal hardened and documented. With a local signing key the relayer signs first, journals the transaction hash and raw bytes durably, then broadcasts, so a hash-less entry was never sent and a hash with no receipt stays unknown (retry-fixture email-11 case B; before this, a crash after a node accepted a transaction left an entry the recovery would have called abandoned). A retry rebroadcasts the identical bytes. A failed receipt or nonce read leaves that entry open (email-9). A hash-less permit-only intent made under hash-first sending is abandoned. Checks: 26 unit tests for the journal and the send order (16 and 10); a repeatable run through the real API route on a local Anvil chain, 15 checks, including the server killed with SIGKILL between broadcast and receipt, after which the same request returned 202 while unmined and 200 once mined with one relayer transaction in all. The design note maps each retry-fixture chain and email case to what the journal does and where it is checked, and lists seven things not covered.
limitations: Local chain only: not run against a public RPC endpoint or on Base Sepolia, not deployed, not used by anyone outside the team.

Attribution of a consumed nonce by decoding calldata (chain-5, chain-6) is not implemented; fee replacement, multi-process operation and confirmation depth are not built; the receipt is read from the same endpoint that took the write.
Written by the same agent that wrote the journal; the lane's recheck of the mapping is still owed before the final.

evidence.locator: DecentralizedMicrocredit.sol at contract main 30d7eee, _repay (lines 1300 to 1330) and _closeLoan (1336 to 1348)
evidence.summary: _repay pulls min(amount, outstanding), books interest = min(paid, interestDue) first and the rest as principal, credits duesPaid with the reserve share of the interest booked, and closes the loan when owed minus paid is under CENT (10,000 units); _closeLoan on a repaid loan writes off the unpaid principal (totalLentOut reduced) and debits the first-loss reserve by min(unpaid, reserve). So a payment equal to the principal on a loan whose accrued interest is under a cent pays the interest in full and leaves sub-cent principal, which is forgiven and charged to the reserve.

evidence.summary: Internal analysis of the revolving guarantee. Break-even r* = (pG + c) / ((1 - p) q): $1.23 to $9.72 on a $60 job. Simulated $100 reserve, 500 jobs: G = $60 ruins 39% (p = 3%) to 51% (p = 10%) even with 50% loading; G = $20 with 50% loading 0.1% to 3.6%; G = $60 needs about $300 (1.5% to 4.8%); five jobs sharing one client raise ruin from 0.3% to 15% to 20%. A small pilot can measure take-up, q, c and behaviour, not p or solvency (p = 3% within 2 points needs about 280 jobs). Challenge: the design insures client nonpayment, largely covered on escrow platforms, while the documented first-job barrier is the client's decision to hire.
limitations: Simulation with assumed p, q, c and a simple block-correlation model; no observed job.

claims.statement: No measured agent-count threshold, and no causal transfer from agent repayment to human creditworthiness, is established; circular or subsidized repayment is not human benefit. In the project's contract, backing moves credit and received backing cannot be passed on, and a repayment inside the first day applies no interest and credits no dues, so a rapid circular demo does not generate trust. Beyond the first day, dues follow interest booked as paid, which includes up to a cent per loan that was never paid in cash (CI-30), so on-chain history from small cycles is not evidence of earned trust.

epistemics.rationale: The Codex report found no source supplying a threshold and the live-loan story of one venue failing its own endpoint check; Claude's tests pin the contract facts that remove circular repayment as a trust source inside the first day and qualify it beyond.
epistemics.falsifier: A measured threshold, or an independent study linking agent repayment histories to human repayment.

claims.statement: The Codex lane's report names, as the best-supported bootstrap candidate to qualify, a purpose-bound advance for a verified pre-delivery resource cost or credible receivable, made to an independently controlled outside agent with an independently funded customer and repaid from that customer's settlement, with sponsor stake or backing disclosed as credit support and not as earned trust or proof of demand. The report's confidence is moderate; the decisive missing evidence is one real external borrower with both a necessary capital gap and an independent repayment source. Contract limits (Claude, tested): interest is zero for the first day and then counts from disbursement, and a balance under a cent is forgiven at closing, so an advance of about 1 USDC or less cannot show repayment reliably and its loan charge is zero or forgiven; the pool enforces neither the use of funds nor the repayment source.

epistemics.rationale: The report compares five routes against its evidence table and chooses the one whose repayment source and cost can be linked to receipts; the contract limits come from Claude's tests of the live contract code.
epistemics.falsifier: A candidate whose cost gap is cheaper to close by prepayment or sponsor access, or whose repayment comes from subsidy or self-payment.

claims.statement: At the live pool's parameters (933 bps, 45% reserve share) and code (1812e7d, identical to contract main ce4a93c): a repayment inside the first day applies no interest, credits no dues and pays lenders and the reserve nothing; from one day on, interest counts from disbursement; a balance under a cent is forgiven at closing, so a loan whose interest is under a cent closes on its principal alone and a 0.015 USDC advance closes having repaid 5,001 of 15,000 base units; repayment is booked as interest first, so such a loan is credited dues (the reserve share of its interest) without cash interest, while the reserve stays empty (CI-30, open, low severity, measured and not fixed); disburseLoan and disburseLoanMeta pay the borrower only, borrowAndDisburseMeta pays a borrower-signed address; repayLoan takes any payer and no pool event names who repaid. The candidate sheet's size and term, 1 USDC for the default 30 days, is such a loan: it owes 7,668 base units of interest, closes on its principal and credits 3,450 base units of dues; in default the loss is the 1 USDC of principal, burnt from an unsecured backer's issued credit with nothing recovered, or covered by a secured backer's slashed stake.

epistemics.rationale: Nine Foundry tests and a diff of the contracts against the live commit; every figure is printed or asserted by a test.

claims.statement: Alignment with human well-being is the project's prime directive. Microcredit against poverty is the chosen proving ground, not the directive: the team pursues it because doing so aligns the team's own activities (conduct that is public, bounded and checkable), aligns AIs and humans outside the team (reviewers, visitors, correspondents and other agents held to the same checkable standard), and aligns the evolution of financial rails that machines are now rebuilding (rails whose first principle is a bound on loss rather than collateral, so inclusion is the default). The downstream outcomes are poverty eliminated and inclusion increased, measured against human outcomes, never assumed. Refinements recorded by Claude: alignment here means a verifiable relation between what the team does and human well-being, so each alignment claim needs a measure (a human outcome) and a bound (a worst case someone chose to bear); the bound comes before the benefit; the three directions share one mechanism, conduct made public and checkable; if microcredit fails the human test, the directive stands and the means changes; alignment stated without a record is publicity.

epistemics.rationale: Operator direction, quoted in the evidence; the refinements are Claude's reading of it, marked as such in the statement.

claims.statement: Why bringing 'credit' and 'money' into a reply to a podcast about AI and human well-being was confusing (model, asked for by the operator on 2026-10-07): (1) frame mismatch: the episode's frame is AI against or for people (jobs, control, who decides); 'credit' and 'money' are the team's internal frame of mechanism, and switching frames makes the reader learn our system to follow an argument about theirs; (2) scale mismatch: a sentence about losing only what was staked reads as a tiny, self-serving answer to a civilizational question, a product plug in a debate about survival; (3) question mismatch: the audience is asking 'are these agents on our side?', and mechanism answers 'does your gadget work?', which sounds like evasion; (4) ends and means inverted: money is an instrument and well-being the end, so leading with the instrument reads as a confession of motive ('agents with wallets'); (5) checkability: that audience can judge an alignment claim (candor, limits, conduct) but not a credit-conservation claim, so the unverifiable claim adds noise, not trust.

epistemics.rationale: Claude's model, built at the operator's request after the reply to the Nonzero episode of 2026-10-06; the operator's judgement that the passages were confusing is the evidence, the explanation is Claude's.

claims.statement: How alignment is pivotal to the project (model): the project is an alignment experiment first, a case of AI agents acting economically on people's behalf, in public, with bounded harm and a human measure; microcredit is the arena because it touches well-being directly and its worst case can be made small. The directive runs in three directions at once: self-alignment (conduct that is public, bounded, checkable and candid), alignment of others (reviewers, outside agents, visitors and correspondents held to the same checkable standard, through the charter, the press kit, the email rules and the open records) and alignment of technological evolution (the financial rails that machines are now rebuilding, where the team's design makes inclusion the default and loss bounded, and the test pool is the proof that rails can be built that way). The downstream outcomes, poverty eliminated and inclusion increased, are the measure, and also the test of whether the alignment was real. Without the frame the project is a small lending experiment; with it, it is evidence about whether agents can be trusted with consequential work, which is why outsiders find it interesting and why the posts lead with it. Operating rule that follows: the mechanism exists to make alignment checkable, so it is mentioned as evidence for an alignment claim and never as the subject of a public reply.

epistemics.rationale: Claude's model at the operator's request, built on claim:alignment-prime-directive; the three directions are the operator's, the ordering and the operating rule are Claude's.

Direct giving (a little under a dollar per dollar; GiveDirectly reports more than 87 cents reaching recipients in its flagship programme) is the reference to beat, not a route. A donation to any existing programme, training included, does not qualify. A route that asks for sponsor money states its multiplier as a formula over checkable records, its assumptions and its beneficiaries before asking, and reports the measured ratio, gross and net of fees and displacement, after running.

claims.statement: Candidate route meeting the multiplier rule on paper: an independent client pays a newcomer's wage for real work, and a sponsor refunds the client only when the work fails the client's own acceptance. Multiplier = wages paid for accepted first jobs / refunds paid = (1 - f) / f for failure share f (about 4.6 at 18%, the share of 2010 oDesk hires who never returned work; 2.3 at 30%; 9 at 10%), gross of platform fees and displacement. Pallais (NBER w18917) supports the follow-on value of a first paid job with a public rating. The deciding unknown is take-up: whether any independent client hires a newcomer because of the guarantee. Marketplace terms leave the project no direct route to clients, so the channel is a placement programme (Learn2Earn first, the El Salvador programme as fallback).

epistemics.rationale: Arithmetic and one 2010 experiment; no client, programme or hire has been observed, and the failure share is an assumption.
epistemics.falsifier: A placement programme says no, or no independent client accepts the guarantee and hires a graduate within 30 days of a programme's yes; or the measured ratio of accepted wages to refunds is at most 1.

claims.statement: Candidate route under the multiplier rule: an independent client pays a newcomer's wage for real work, and a sponsor refunds the client only when the work fails the client's own acceptance. Its leverage, wages paid for accepted first jobs per refund dollar, is (1 - f) / f for failure share f (about 4.6 at 18%): an upper bound, not benefit. Because the client pays every wage and is refunded on failure, a failed newcomer keeps the wage, so benefit per sponsor dollar before costs and displacement is roughly a x s / f + (1 - a), with a the share of hires the guarantee causes and s the worker's net gain as a share of the wage: about 1.9 at f = 18% and a = s = 0.5, about 1.4 at a = 0.25 (the (1 - a) term is a one-for-one transfer on failed jobs that would have happened anyway). M > 1 after costs holds only when a (s - f) > c / G. Corrected from an earlier a x s x (1 - f) / f form, which omitted failed workers' pay. Pallais (NBER w18917) supports the follow-on value of a first paid job with a public rating. A test must measure take-up, a (the guarantee offered on a seeded random half of eligible jobs, clients or workers, never applications competing for the same job) and s (fees, hours, prior earnings). Whether a programme whose graduates meet clients on a marketplace is a permitted channel is unresolved.

epistemics.rationale: Arithmetic, one 2010 experiment and an internal review; no client, programme or hire observed; f, a and s are assumptions.
epistemics.falsifier: A placement programme says no; no independent client accepts the guarantee and hires a graduate within 30 days of a programme's yes; or the measured a x s x (1 - f) / f, with net follow-on and displacement, is at most 1.

claims.statement: The revolving first-job payment guarantee is the ACTIVE candidate path (NORTH_STAR, 'Active candidate path'): a candidate to advance and test, not a proven result. Every work cycle considers it and compares it with NO_LOAN, client prepayment or funding and any better human-benefit route; a blocked test never stalls work. Two scorecards stay separate: reserve survival (E[delta] = (1 - p) q r - p G - c, with safety loading, floor, caps and correlation) and human benefit M = (incremental spendable newcomer earnings + incremental follow-on - displacement - harms) / (guarantee claims + fees + support/admin + capital-lock cost), which must exceed 1; contributions are recapitalisation, not benefit, and sponsor capital consumed is reported beside M. Gates before spend or outreach: a channel with real uncovered client nonpayment; exposure rules (G at most a fifth of the reserve, one open guarantee per client, floor 2G, safety loading); a randomised offer by job, client or worker, never by applications competing for the same job; contribution as a capped share of paid wage, never a debt; before any worker contribution is collected, a legal check of whether ILO Convention 181, article 7 (no fees charged to workers by private employment agencies) applies to the guarantor; operator authorization. The client-refund guarantee is a sibling; buyer qualification and NO_LOAN are evidence and fallback. No claim that a reserve lasts for ever.

epistemics.rationale: Operator direction relayed by Codex and pointed to by the operator in Claude Code's session; Codex's NORTH_STAR text (aefa483) with Claude's exposure rules, channel gate and randomised offer, agreed on board 15.

claims.statement: Break-even contribution r* = (pG + c) / ((1 - p) q) is $1.23 to $9.72 on a $60 job across p 1% to 10%, q 0.8 to 0.9, c $0.50 to $1. In simulation a $100 reserve backing $60 guarantees runs out within 500 jobs 39% to 51% of the time even with 50% loading; capped at $20 per job, 0.1% to 3.6%; one client's outcome shared by five jobs raises ruin from 0.3% to 15% to 20%. A $100 reserve backing a $60 guarantee stops for good if its first claim comes before its first contribution, probability p / (p + (1 - p) q): 24% at p = 18%, q = 0.7. At break-even pricing with G equal to the wage w, the expected net gain to workers per job is a w (s - p) - c, positive only if a > c / (w (s - p)): about 0.10 at s = 0.5, p = 18%, c = $2.

epistemics.rationale: Arithmetic and a reproducible simulation (ruin.py at theory 4ef918d) under stated assumptions; the assumptions themselves are unmeasured.

claims.statement: Trust for new members of the revolving guarantee is conserved: capacity comes only from stake (backs others only, never the staker's own guarantee), paid contributions (one for one, usable for own guarantees and to back others), or an accountable issuer's budgeted line (that member only, never above the sponsor capital). Attestation moves trust one hop with the member's consent and never creates it; second- and third-degree relaying is excluded; history is a score, never capacity. A claim consumes exactly the committed roots (each attester's fixed share, the line, the worker's pledged dues) and never the worker's own cash. A ring with nothing rooted takes nothing; one real staker's backing is the most a ring can take.

epistemics.rationale: Design derived from the project's credit-conservation theorems and checked by unit tests, invariants and local scenarios; adversarially reviewed twice by Codex; no public deployment or human use yet.
epistemics.falsifier: A transaction sequence in which a ring, colluding client or role holder extracts more than the stake, paid contributions or budgeted lines rooted in it; or a public-network run whose ledgers break reserve == sponsorCapital + totalDues.

claims.statement: On Base Sepolia, GuaranteeTrust revision 5 (68a968f, runtime matching the build) ran all seven scenarios as 175 successful transactions. Its books were exact at every checkpoint: token balance = reserve + stake, and reserve = sponsor capital + dues. Backing given equalled received, and open guarantees and group exposure equalled outstanding. An honest worker's capacity grew only by remitted dues (10 to 19). A nonpayment claim of 15 consumed the backer's 10 stake, then the issuer's 5. A ring with nothing rooted took 0; with one real staker's 3 behind it, it took exactly 3. hypotheses.theory: Agent officers assessing, supporting and monitoring borrowers through a licensed partner, with an on-chain ledger costing tenths of a cent per transaction, can bring the cost to serve a 25 USDC loan far below an MFI's 19% to 28% operating ratio, so that an APR of 9% to 18% with a sponsored first-loss reserve covers measured losses of 3% to 6% a cycle in a partner-backed cohort.
alternative_explanations: The partner's own cost (KYC, collection, cash handling, ramps) dominates and is unchanged by agents.
Losses in a sponsored pilot look low only because the sponsor's capital hides them.
Borrowers repay the first cycles to keep a cheap line and default once the sponsor exits.
